title: The One Million Yuan on the Signature Page
teaser: The company’s assets are valued at 1.26 million yuan today, against a debt of only 1.00 million due in a year, so the refinancing appears to meet the initial test. But after settling three possible maturity states—700,000, 1.00 million, and 1.40 million—Zhou Lan sees that the same one-million-yuan line does not mean the same thing on both sides of it.
paragraphs: At 4:10 on Friday afternoon, Yuanhang Company was still waiting for one signature on its refinancing. Its owner, Chen Hai, needed the approval before the bank closed so that he could renew the next year’s transport contract together with the ship financing. The papers on loan manager Zhou Lan’s desk did not look alarming. The company’s main asset was a single cargo vessel and the transport contract tied to it, with a latest valuation of 1.26 million yuan. A debt of 1.00 million yuan would fall due in one lump sum a year later, with no interim interest and no other senior debt. Under the simplified first screen used for this refinancing, the assets still covered the debt today.

Zhou Lan paused when she reached the guarantee page. Chen Hai had given no unlimited personal guarantee, so what the bank could recover at maturity would ultimately depend on what assets the company still had then. Xu, the accountant, took an old metal box used for the ship’s papers from a cabinet. He laid the 1.00-million-yuan note at the bottom and cut three stiff cards marked 700,000, 1.00 million, and 1.40 million. On the back of each card Zhou Lan wrote, “Maturity state, not probability.” She did not alter the current 1.26-million valuation or guess which card was more likely. She simply asked Xu to settle the three maturity states one by one.

The 1.40-million card went down first. Xu laid out paper money representing 1.40 million yuan, pushed 1.00 million to the bank’s side, and left the remaining 400,000 in front of Chen Hai. Next came 1.00 million. The money on the table covered the note exactly, leaving Chen Hai’s side empty. Chen Hai looked at the two arrangements and drew the signing pen from the folder. In both states, the bank received everything it was owed; in the first, the shareholders still kept 400,000 yuan.

The last card was 700,000. Xu laid out only 700,000 yuan and pushed it all toward Zhou Lan. The “1,000,000” on the note was still partly visible, leaving a shortfall of 300,000. Chen Hai’s side was still simply zero. It did not become minus 300,000, and there was no separate pool of personal property to fill the gap. Zhou Lan did not change the 700,000 card or treat it as a forecast of trouble. She pressed the pen Chen Hai had just taken out back into the folder and lined up all three cards.

In the blank space on the approval sheet, she drew two columns and copied only the payouts they had just placed on the table: with assets at 700,000, the bank received 700,000 and shareholders zero; at 1.00 million, the bank received 1.00 million and shareholders zero; at 1.40 million, the bank received 1.00 million and shareholders 400,000. She then checked the line that read “current asset value: 1.26 million yuan.” The number had not changed. What had changed was the line beneath it. Above 1.00 million, additional value continued to fall to the shareholders. Below 1.00 million, the shareholders’ column stopped falling, while the bank’s recovery began to decline with the assets. The original screen—“1.26 is greater than 1.00”—was not wrong, but it was no longer enough for a judgment meant to hold for the whole year.

At 4:52, Zhou Lan still signed the refinancing. She did not reject the transaction because of the 700,000 state. Instead, she changed the loan-period requirements: the value of the ship and contract, together with estimates of their volatility, would be updated regularly, and the terms would be reviewed early if asset value approached the 1.00-million-yuan debt due at maturity, rather than waiting for the next annual static valuation. Xu returned the 700,000 and 1.40-million cards to the metal box. Zhou Lan left the 1.00-million card on top of the approval sheet. Before closing the folder, she took a ruler and drew a straight line under “1,000,000.”
concept: Under a simplified capital structure, the Merton structural credit model treats equity as a call-option-like claim on the firm’s assets, with debt D due at maturity acting as the exercise threshold. If asset value V at maturity is above D, creditors receive D and shareholders receive V−D. If V is below D, shareholder payoff stops at zero and creditors can recover only the remaining asset value. Thus shareholder payoff at maturity is max(V−D, 0), while creditor recovery is min(V, D).
explanation: The point is not to decide whether 700,000, 1.00 million, or 1.40 million is more likely. It is to see how the same change in asset value is allocated at maturity: value above 1.00 million accrues to shareholders, while below 1.00 million the asset shortfall begins to reduce creditor recovery and shareholder payoff does not fall below zero.
mapping: Current valuation of 1.26 million yuan and debt of 1.00 million due in one year → On a static view, assets still cover the debt, but today’s coverage does not directly reveal how payoffs will be divided at maturity.

No unlimited personal guarantee and no other senior debt → The story is limited to a simplified capital structure with limited liability, so the bank can recover only from the company’s assets at maturity.
Three “maturity state” cards marked 700,000, 1.00 million, and 1.40 million → They illustrate different maturity asset values V, not three probabilities.

The bank/shareholder columns of 700/0, 1,000/0, and 1,000/400 → They show the creditor payoff capped at D, the shareholder payoff floored at zero, and the asymmetric allocation on the two sides of the 1.00-million-yuan threshold.
boundary: The story illustrates only the most basic maturity-payoff mechanism of the Merton structural credit model; it is not a complete firm-value estimate or default-probability calculation. A full model also requires estimates of asset value, asset volatility, the risk-free rate, and time to maturity, and it depends on assumptions such as a simplified capital structure. Real firms may also have multiple debt layers, guarantees, restructuring, early default, and disposal costs. The 700,000, 1.00-million, and 1.40-million figures are illustrative states, not probabilities.
reflection: If the current valuation of 1.26 million yuan did not change, why did Zhou Lan still change the way the loan would be monitored after seeing the three maturity payouts?

calculation.formula: Shareholder payoff at maturity = max(V−D, 0), D=1.00 million yuan
calculation.V70: Creditors 700,000 yuan, shortfall 300,000 yuan; shareholders 0 yuan
